butir.teks: Similar to this is the saying of Allah Most High, ⟦QS 21:18⟧ And in the report: "What I fear for my community is only the slip of a scholar."

and the disputation of a hypocrite about the Qur'an. (١) Among them is that his concern is to acquire the knowledge that benefits in the Hereafter and encourages obedience, avoiding the sciences whose benefit is little and in which disputation and idle talk abound.

So the example of one who turns away from the knowledge of deeds and busies himself with disputation is that of a sick man with many ailments who has met a skilled physician at a time that is short and that he fears will pass, and he busies himself with asking about the properties of drugs and medicines and the curiosities of medicine, and leaves his pressing concern for which he is held to account. That is sheer foolishness.

The third: I looked at this creation and saw that everyone who has something of value and worth lifts it away and guards it. Then I looked at the saying of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, ⟦QS 16:96⟧ so whenever something of value and worth came to me, I directed it to Allah so that it would remain preserved with Him.

The fourth: I looked at this creation and saw each of them falling back on wealth, on ancestral standing, honour, and lineage. I considered them, and behold, they are nothing. Then I looked at the saying of Allah Most High, ⟦QS 49:13⟧ so I worked at God-consciousness (taqwa) until I would be noble with Allah.

The fifth: I looked at this creation, and they were attacking one another and cursing one another, and the root of all this is envy. Then I looked at the saying of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, ⟦QS 43:32⟧ so I gave up envy, avoided people, and knew that the apportionment is from Allah, glorified and exalted is He, so I put aside people's enmity toward me.

The sixth: I looked at this creation, some of them transgressing against others and some fighting others, so I returned to the saying of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, ⟦QS 35:6⟧ so I made an enemy of him alone and strove to take my guard against him, because Allah Most High bore witness against him that he is an enemy to me, so I gave up enmity toward anyone else in creation.

The seventh: I looked at this creation and saw each of them seeking this morsel of bread, humbling himself for it and entering into what is not lawful for him. Then I looked at the saying of Allah Most High, ⟦QS 11:6⟧ so I knew that I am one of these creatures whose provision is upon Allah, so I busied myself with what Allah Most High has upon me and left what I have with Him.

The eighth: I looked at this creation and saw all of them relying on a created being: this one on his estate, this one on his trade, this one on his craft, and this one on the health of his body; and every created being relies on one like himself. So I returned to

the saying of Allah Most High, ⟦QS 65:3⟧ so I relied on Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and He is sufficient for me." Shaqiq said, "Hatim, may Allah Most High grant you success! I have looked into the sciences of the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms, and the great Furqan, and I found all kinds of good and religion, and they revolve around these eight matters. Whoever puts them into practice has put the four books into practice." This kind of knowledge is cared about, grasped, and discerned only by the scholars of the Hereafter. As for the scholars of this world, they busy themselves with what makes the earning of wealth and status easy, and neglect the like of these sciences with which Allah sent all the prophets (peace be upon them). Ad-Dahhak ibn Muzahim said, "I met them, and they learned from one another only scrupulousness (wara'), whereas today they learn only theology (kalam)." Among them is that he is not inclined to luxury in food and drink, ease in clothing, and adornment in furnishings and dwelling; rather he prefers moderation in all of this and imitates the early generations (salaf) (may Allah Most High have mercy on them) in it, and inclines to be content with less in all of it. The more his inclination goes to the side of fewness, the more his nearness to Allah increases and the higher his company rises among the scholars of the Hereafter.

Evidence for that is what is related of Abu Abd Allah al-Khawwas, who was one of the companions of Hatim al-Asamm. He said, "I entered ar-Rayy with Hatim, and with us were three hundred and twenty men intending the pilgrimage (hajj), wearing zarmanaqat, with no provision bag and no food among them. We went to a man of the merchants, an austere man who loved the poor, and he hosted us that night. The next day he said to Hatim, 'Do you have a need? For I want to visit a jurist of ours who is ill.' Hatim said, 'Visiting the sick has merit, and looking at a jurist is worship. I will come with you as well.'"

The sick man was Muhammad ibn Muqatil, the judge of ar-Rayy. When we came to the door, behold, a lofty, beautiful palace, and Hatim remained in thought, saying, "The door of a scholar in this state!" Then they were given permission and entered, and behold, a beautiful house, and beyond it a spacious, pleasant expanse, and apparel and curtains. Hatim remained in thought. Then they entered the room where he was, and behold, soft bedding, and he was lying on it, and at his head a servant boy with a fly whisk in his hand. The merchant sat at his head and asked about his condition while Hatim stood. Ibn Muqatil motioned to him to sit. Hatim said, "I will not sit." Ibn Muqatil said, "Perhaps you have a need?" Hatim said, "Yes." Ibn Muqatil said, "And what is it?" Hatim said, "A question I want to ask you." Ibn Muqatil said, "Ask." Hatim said, "Get up and sit upright so that I may ask you."

So he sat upright. Hatim said, "This knowledge of yours, from where did you take it?" Ibn Muqatil said, "From trustworthy people; they narrated it to me." Hatim said, "From whom?" He said, "From the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him)." Hatim said, "And the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him), from whom?" He said, "From the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him)." Hatim said, "And the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him), from whom?" He said, "From Gabriel (peace be upon him), from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic."

Hatim said, "Then in what Gabriel (peace be upon him) conveyed from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, to the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him), and the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) conveyed to his Companions, and his Companions to the trustworthy, and the trustworthy conveyed to you, have you heard that whoever has height in his house and its spaciousness is greater has a greater station with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic?" Ibn Muqatil said, "No." Hatim said, "How then did you hear?" He said, "I heard that whoever renounces this world, desires the Hereafter, loves the poor, and sends ahead for his Hereafter has the station with Allah." Hatim said to him, "Then whom did you follow? The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) and his Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) and the righteous (may Allah have mercy on them), or Pharaoh and Nimrod, the first to build with gypsum and baked brick? O evil scholars, the like of you is seen by the ignorant man who clamours for this world and desires it, and he says, 'The scholar is in this state, so should I not be worse than he?'" And he left him, and Ibn Muqatil's illness increased. What had passed between Hatim and Ibn Muqatil reached the people of ar-Rayy, and they said to Hatim, "At-Tanafisi in Qazwin has more lavish means than he."

So Hatim set out deliberately and went in to at-Tanafisi and said, "May Allah have mercy on you. I am a non-Arab man; I would like you to teach me the beginning of my religion and the key to my prayer: how do I perform ablution (wudu') for the prayer?" He said, "Gladly and with honour. Boy, bring a vessel with water in it."

The boy brought it, and at-Tanafisi sat and performed ablution, washing three times each, then said, "Like this you perform ablution." Hatim said, "Stay where you are, so that I may perform ablution in front of you, for that will make what I want more firmly fixed." So at-Tanafisi got up and Hatim sat and performed ablution, then washed his arms four times each. At-Tanafisi said, "Man, you have been wasteful." Hatim said to him, "In what?" He said, "You washed your arms four times." Hatim said, "Glory be to Allah, the Mighty! I, with a handful of water, was wasteful, and you, in all of this, were not wasteful?" So at-Tanafisi knew

that he had intended that and not to learn. He went into his house and did not come out to the people for forty days. When Hatim entered Baghdad, the people of Baghdad gathered to him and said, "Abu Abd ar-Rahman, you are a man, but a non-Arab, and no one speaks to you without you silencing him." He said, "I have three qualities with which I prevail over my opponent: I rejoice when my opponent is right, I grieve when he errs, and I guard myself against acting ignorantly towards him."
That reached the Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and he said, "Glory be to Allah, how intelligent he is! Get up, let us go to him."

When they went in to him, Ahmad said to him, "Abu Abd ar-Rahman, what is safety from this world?" Hatim said, "Abu Abd Allah, you are not safe from this world until you have four qualities: you forgive the people their ignorance, you keep your own ignorance away from them, you give them of what is yours, and you are without hope of what is theirs. If you are like this, you are safe." Then he travelled to Medina, and the people of Medina met him. He said, "People, what city is this?" They said, "The city of the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him)." He said, "Then where is the palace of the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him), so that I may pray in it?" They said, "He had no palace; he had only a house close to the ground." He said, "Then where are the palaces of his Companions (may Allah be pleased with them)?" They said, "They had no palaces; they had only houses close to the ground." Hatim said, "People, then this is the city of Pharaoh!" So they seized him and took him to the ruler and said, "This non-Arab says this is the city of Pharaoh." The governor said, "Why is that?" Hatim said, "Do not rush me. I am a non-Arab, a stranger. I entered the town and said, 'Whose city is this?' and they said, 'The city of the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him).' I said, 'Then where is the palace of'" and he related the story. Then he said, "And Allah Most High said, ⟦QS 33:21⟧ So whom have you taken as your example? The Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him), or Pharaoh, the first to build with gypsum and baked brick?" So they let him go and left him alone.
This, then, is the story of Hatim al-Asamm (may Allah Most High have mercy on him).

What bears witness to that will come in its places, from the conduct of the early generations concerning plain dress (badhadha) and abandoning adornment. The accurate position on it is that adorning oneself with what is permissible is not forbidden, but plunging into it brings familiarity with it until leaving it becomes hard. And keeping up adornment is not possible except by engaging in means, and in most cases attending to them necessarily leads to committing acts of disobedience: flattery, regard for people and showing off to them, and other matters that are forbidden. Prudence is to avoid that, because whoever plunges into this world does not at all escape it. Had safety been on offer together with plunging into it, the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) would not have gone to extremes in leaving this world, to the point of taking off the shirt embroidered with a pattern (١) and taking off the gold ring in the middle of the sermon (٢), and other things whose explanation will come.

It is related that Yahya ibn Yazid an-Nawfali wrote to Malik ibn Anas (may Allah be pleased with them both): "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. May Allah bless His Messenger Muhammad among the first and the last. From Yahya ibn Yazid ibn Abd al-Malik to Malik ibn Anas. To proceed: it has reached me that you wear fine clothes, eat thin bread, sit on soft bedding, and set a doorkeeper at your door, while you have taken your seat in the assembly of knowledge, and riding beasts have been driven to you, and people have travelled to you, and taken you as an imam and been satisfied with your word. So fear Allah Most High, Malik, and hold to humility. I have written to you, as advice from me, a letter that none but Allah, glorified and exalted is He, has seen. Peace." Malik wrote to him: "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. May Allah bless our master Muhammad, his family and his Companions, and grant them peace. From Malik ibn Anas to Yahya ibn Yazid. The peace of Allah be upon you. To proceed: your letter has reached me, and it fell with me in the place of advice, compassion, and good conduct. May Allah let you enjoy God-consciousness (taqwa) and reward you well for the advice, and I ask Allah Most High for success, and there is no might and no power except with Allah, the Most High, the Almighty. As for what you mentioned to me, that I eat thin bread, wear fine clothes, keep a doorkeeper, and sit on soft bedding, we do that and we seek forgiveness of Allah Most High, for Allah Most High has said, ⟦QS 7:32⟧ And I know that leaving that is better than getting into it. Do not cease writing to us, for we will not cease writing to you. Peace." So look at Malik's fairness, in that he admitted that

leaving that is better than getting into it, and gave the ruling that it is permissible, and he was truthful in both. A man like Malik in his standing, if his self is generous with fairness and admission in such advice, then his self also finds strength to stop at the limits of the permissible, so that this does not lead him to showing off, flattery, and going beyond into disliked matters (makruh). But someone other than him is not able to do so. Lingering over indulgence in the permissible is a great danger and far from fear and awe. And the distinctive mark of the scholars of Allah Most High is awe, and the distinctive mark of awe is keeping far from the places where danger is likely.

Among them is that he keeps far from rulers and does not enter upon them at all as long as he finds a way to flee from them; rather he ought to guard against mixing with them even if they come to him, for this world is sweet and green, and its reins are in the hands of rulers.
And one who mixes with them is not free of forced effort in seeking their good pleasure and winning over their hearts, even though they are wrongdoers.

It is obligatory for every religious person to denounce them and to distress them by making their wrongdoing evident and making their conduct appear ugly. The one who enters upon them either turns to their finery and so belittles the blessing of Allah upon him, or stays silent instead of denouncing them and so becomes one who flatters them, or contrives in his speech words to please them and to beautify their state, and that is plain slander, or covets to obtain some of their worldly goods, and that is unlawful gain (suht). In the Book of the Lawful and the Forbidden there will come what may and may not be taken from the wealth of rulers, of stipends, gifts, and the like.
In sum, mixing with them is a key to evils, and the way of the scholars of the Hereafter is caution.

The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said, "Whoever lives in the desert becomes rough" - meaning whoever dwells in the desert becomes harsh - "and whoever follows the hunt becomes heedless, and whoever comes to the ruler is put to trial." (١) And he (peace and blessings be upon him) said, "There will be rulers over you among whom you will find what you recognise and what you reject. Whoever rejects has been absolved, and whoever dislikes has been safe; but whoever is pleased and follows, Allah Most High will keep him far away." It was said, "Should we not fight them?" He (peace and blessings be upon him) said, "No, as long as they pray." (٢) And Sufyan said, "In Hell there is a valley in which only the reciters who visit kings dwell."

Hudhayfa said, "Beware of the places of trials." It was said, "What are they?" He said, "The doors of the emirs. One of you enters upon the emir and confirms him in a lie and says of him what is not in him."

The Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) said, "The scholars are the trustees of the messengers over Allah's servants as long as they do not mix with rulers. If they do that, they have betrayed the messengers, so beware of them and withdraw from them." (٣) Anas related it.

Al-A'mash was told, "You have revived knowledge, because of the many who take it from you." He said, "Do not be hasty: a third die before attaining it, a third keep to the doors of rulers, and they are the worst of creation, and of the remaining third only a few succeed." For that reason Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib (may Allah have mercy on him) said, "If you see a scholar frequenting emirs, be on guard against him, for he is a thief."
Al-Awza'i said, "There is nothing more hateful to Allah Most High than a scholar who visits a governor."

The Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) said, "The worst of the scholars are those who come to the emirs, and the best of the emirs are those who come to the scholars." (٤) And Makhul ad-Dimashqi (may Allah have mercy on him) said, "Whoever learns the Qur'an and gains understanding in religion, then keeps company with a ruler out of flattery towards him and greed for what he has, wades into a sea of the fire of Hell according to the number of his steps."

Sumnun said, "How repulsive it is for a scholar that his gathering is come to and he is not found, and it is asked about him and it is said, 'He is with the emir.'" He said, "I used to hear it said, 'If you see a scholar who loves this world, suspect him regarding your religion,' until I tried that myself: I never once entered upon this ruler without taking myself to account after leaving, and I find liability upon it. And you see the harshness, the bluntness, and the frequent opposition to his whim with which I meet him, and I would like to escape from going in to him breaking even, even though I take nothing from him and do not drink a drink of water from him."
Then he said, "The scholars of our time are worse than the scholars of the Children of Israel: they tell the ruler of the concessions and of what agrees with

his whim. Had they told him what is against him and in which is his salvation, he would find them burdensome and dislike their entering upon him, and that would be salvation for them with their Lord."
